claims.text: The initial material is a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate.
Increasing chromium content promotes formation of a stable chromium-oxide surface layer.
Increasing chromium content enhances the coating's oxidation resistance.
The chromium-rich oxide layer acts as a protective layer during sliding.
The protective oxide layer reduces wear.
The protective oxide layer limits microscopic deformation.
A higher-chromium coating will have better wear resistance than the baseline lower-chromium coating under otherwise identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
A higher-chromium coating will exhibit less microscopic deformation than the baseline lower-chromium coating under otherwise identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
The predicted effects apply in a high-temperature regime where oxidation significantly affects sliding wear.
The relationship between chromium content and wear resistance may depend on the other alloying elements and microstructural factors.
Wear-volume loss can be used to compare wear performance between the baseline and increased-chromium coatings.
Surface roughness or microhardness can be used as measurements of microscopic deformation.
A lack of significant improvement in both wear resistance and microscopic deformation for the increased-chromium coating would falsify the hypothesis.
